Rising to the height of a large dog, the mud covered salamander slinks through marshes and wetlands, its long sharpened tongue 
tucked into its odd jaw-less mouth. Th is amphibian, like its smaller cousins, needs a wet environment to survive and, because of its 
larger size, often rests in shallow ponds or in the muddy silt of swamps, awaiting the sounds of approaching prey. Evolving a powerful 
harpoon-like tongue that became too large and long to fi t within its mouth, the bottom jaw receded to simple vestigial bones that rest 
beneath the jaw. When prey draws near, a whip-fast bone edged tongue rips out of the mud, stretching a full 10 feet to impale and 
embed its barb deeply into the unfortunate creature. Just as quickly, the salamander reels it into its awaiting needle toothed maw.
